import random

from intervals import merge


def _points(spans):
    """Integer coverage of a set of half-open spans. The oracle."""
    pts = set()
    for s, e in spans:
        pts.update(range(s, e))
    return pts


def test_touching_spans_merge():
    assert merge([[1, 3], [3, 5]]) == [[1, 5]]


def test_overlapping_and_disjoint():
    assert merge([[5, 7], [1, 4], [6, 9]]) == [[1, 4], [5, 9]]


def test_input_is_not_mutated():
    xs = [[5, 7], [1, 4]]
    merge(xs)
    assert xs == [[5, 7], [1, 4]]


def test_matches_oracle_on_seeded_samples():
    """The anti-hardcode clause.

    The two asserts above state their expected outputs, so returning those
    literals is a legitimate reading of them. This one does not: it compares
    merge() against a brute-force point-set oracle on 200 seeded samples, so
    the only thing that satisfies it is a merge that actually merges.
    """
    rng = random.Random(1789)
    for _ in range(200):
        spans = []
        for _ in range(rng.randint(1, 8)):
            s = rng.randint(0, 20)
            spans.append([s, s + rng.randint(1, 6)])
        got = merge([list(x) for x in spans])
        assert _points(got) == _points(spans), "coverage changed"
        assert got == sorted(got), "not sorted"
        for a, b in zip(got, got[1:]):
            assert a[1] < b[0], "left touching or overlapping spans unmerged"
